Common echymipera (Echymipera kalubu) is a moderate-sized peramelemorphian marsupial distributed across lowland rainforests of New Guinea and adjacent islands. Under standard thermoneutral conditions of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], newborns emerge after a remarkably swift gestation period measured at 13 days [tg = 13 days], a duration consistent with the brief pregnancies typical of bandicoots. At parturition, the altricial neonate weighs a mere 0.25 grams [Wwb = 0.25 grams], reflecting the extreme altriciality and limited maternal provisioning prior to the fully marsupial phase of development. This tiny birth mass is among the poorest documented for any mammal relative to adult body size. The suckling joey is carried in the pouch for an extended period before emerging to a transitional state, and during this phase the mother provides continuous lactational support. Mean litter size from field captures averages 2.1 pups per litter [N_R_i = 2.1 pups per litter], and females can produce up to three litters each year [F_R_i = up to three litters each year], a reproductive tempo that yields a high annual reproductive output unusual for a marsupial of this lineage.

As the dependent young continues to develop within the maternal pouch, the onset of nutritional independence occurs when the juvenile begins ingesting solid food items. Weaning, marking the cessation of milk ingestion and the transition to an exclusively solid diet, is completed at approximately 60 days after birth [tx = approximately 60 days after birth] under the typical thermal regime of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], a relatively abbreviated suckling period for a marsupial of this body size. At the point of weaning, the juvenile has attained a wet body mass of about 100 grams [Wwx = about 100 grams], a substantial increase over the initial birth mass. This growth trajectory is fueled by the protein-rich milk that bandicoots produce, which supports rapid somatic development during the pouch young stage. After weaning, the young animal becomes independent and forages on its own, consuming a diet dominated by invertebrates, fallen fruit, and underground fungi. The period of maternal investment, from birth through the completion of weaning, is thus compressed relative to many other peramelemorphians, a feature that may facilitate the species' ability to breed in disturbed habitats and maintain stable populations.

Sexual maturity in Common echymipera is reached after a post-weaning development interval under standardized conditions. At the species' characteristic body temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], puberty occurs at 200 days after birth [tp = 200 days after birth], a value that represents the time since birth at gonadal maturation. At this developmental milestone, the individual has attained a wet body mass of approximately 400 grams [Wwp = approximately 400 grams], marking the transition to reproductive competence. This pubertal mass represents roughly half the ultimate adult size and is associated with the onset of spermatogenesis in males and the first ovulation in females. The timing of sexual maturation is relatively rapid compared to that of many dasyuromorphian marsupials of similar size, likely reflecting the selective pressures of a fluctuating environment where early reproduction enhances lifetime fitness. Available data from captive colonies indicate that individuals begin exhibiting courting behaviors and successful copulations shortly after reaching this developmental landmark, confirming that functional reproductive capacity coincides closely with the attainment of pubertal mass.

The ultimate adult size reached by Common echymipera is modest relative to other large bandicoots, with fully grown individuals attaining a maximum wet body mass of 800 grams [Wwi = 800 grams]. This asymptotic mass is supported by a relatively low resting metabolic rate, measured under thermoneutral conditions as 344 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 344 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This basal oxygen consumption value is consistent with the reduced mass-specific metabolic demands typical of tropical mammals, which often exhibit lower BMRs than their temperate counterparts. The species demonstrates a body mass range from approximately 600 grams to 1.2 kilograms in the wild, though most adults gravitate toward the 800-gram endpoint. Adult body mass appears to be influenced by local food abundance, with individuals inhabiting higher-quality alluvial lowland forests tending to achieve larger ultimate sizes than those from disturbed or montane sites. Despite this variation, the 800-gram typical maximum represents a useful interspecific reference point for comparative life-history analyses within the Peramelidae.

Longevity data for Common echymipera are derived primarily from captive records, although field recapture studies provide supplementary information. Under the conditions of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], the maximum recorded life span stands at approximately 6.1 years [am = approximately 6.1 years], well beyond the 2.7 years documented for a single captive individual in an earlier, shorter-duration study. This moderate life span is characteristic of many small to medium-sized marsupials and reflects a fast-paced life history strategy that includes early reproduction, high annual fecundity, and moderate mortality rates in the wild. Field observations suggest that few individuals survive beyond their second year in natural habitats, with predation by feral cats, pythons, and raptors representing significant sources of extrinsic mortality. The species' reproductive rate, expressed on an annual basis as approximately 6.3 pups per female per year, underscores the importance of high recruitment in sustaining populations despite elevated adult turnover. Comparative analyses indicate that Common echymipera conforms to the general peramelid pattern of a short lifespan coupled with synchronized, seasonal breeding bouts.
